name: Cynosure RingBuf (async-native SPSC ring buffer, Rust)
baseline: rigtorp::SPSCQueue (C++ single-producer single-consumer ring buffer). The same table also holds a hand-rolled C11 cached-index ring, which is faster than Cynosure.
workload: Single-thread push plus pop latency of an SPSC ring buffer, measured in a tight loop with LTO and DoNotOptimize against the C++ reference and a bare C11 ring; the same BENCHMARKS.md file also ranks the crate against Rust channels (rtrb, kanal, crossbeam, flume, tokio mpsc) on throughput and cross-thread latency.
claimed_speedup: Single-thread push+pop latency: Cynosure 1.29 ns vs rigtorp::SPSCQueue 2.46 ns (about 1.9x lower, derived from page data); the hand-rolled C11 ring is faster at 0.79 ns (about 1.6x lower than Cynosure). BENCHMARKS.md: 'cynosure is the fastest async-native SPSC queue measured ... beats the canonical C++ library (rigtorp) on latency'. The same file's cross-crate criterion table gives Cynosure 2.2 ns per push+pop and rtrb 2.5 ns.
compiler_and_flags: Rust stable, cargo bench with release plus LTO (README). The C++ and C comparison is described only as a 'maximally-tuned tight loop (LTO, DoNotOptimize)'; C++ compiler, version and flags are not stated.
stars_or_usage: 3 stars; cynosure crate has about 59.6k crates.io downloads
tradeoffs: Rust crate, so use from C++ needs FFI or a separate process. Tuned on AArch64: the benchmark file notes the SeqCst publish store is free on Apple silicon and a barrier on x86, and that numbers 'are very different on x86'. The async-native design pays about one atomic load and a branch per operation to check for a waiting task, which is why a bare synchronous C ring stays faster. Sibling primitives (LocalMutex, LocalSemaphore, triple_buffer, bip_buffer, oneshot, mpsc_light) are for thread-per-core executors such as monoio and glommio.
caveats: The C++ and C11 comparison code is not in the repository: benches/ lists only .rs files and neither the benches README nor spsc_compare.rs mentions rigtorp, so the C++ rows cannot be reproduced, and the C++ compiler and flags are unstated (hence tier C, not A). The 1.29 ns figure comes from a different harness than the 2.2 ns figure in the cross-crate table for the same operation. Single representative run on one Apple laptop-class chip; the file warns that a full cargo bench run thermally throttles later benches by about 15% and that CIs are tight but absolute values vary run to run. The win over rigtorp is on single-thread latency only (a push+pop on one thread, not a producer and consumer on two cores); the project's own text says a bare synchronous C ring beats it by about 1.6x on that path. Very young project (commits visible from July 2025, 3 stars, one author). Found through a README claim, not an independent measurement.
found_via: crates.io API harvest of about 100 concurrency keyword queries (spsc, channel, lock-free, thread-per-core and others), then a grep of about 5,600 crate READMEs for C++ comparator names (rigtorp, moodycamel, folly, boost, libuv, seastar); the Cynosure README line 'beating every async channel, and even rigtorp::SPSCQueue on latency' surfaced it; opened README.md, BENCHMARKS.md, benches/README.md, benches/spsc_compare.rs and the GitHub repo and commits pages.
why_faster: README and BENCHMARKS.md name the cached-index, cache-line-padded ring design (the same family as rtrb and rigtorp::SPSCQueue) and a waiter check that costs one atomic load and branch per call (free on AArch64 ldarb); neither says why 1.29 ns beats rigtorp's 2.46 ns.

name: Myelon / disruptor-mp (shared-memory ring-buffer IPC transport, Rust)
baseline: Boost.Interprocess message_queue ('Boost-MQ', C++) and an Open MPI shared-memory ping-pong (C, built with mpicc); the same chart also holds Rust and Java-ecosystem peers (iceoryx2, Aeron through rusteron, shmipc-rs, crossbeam, ZeroMQ).
workload: Two-process 1p1c ping-pong of 1 KB messages over shared memory or mmap, reported as messages per second, run by the project's competitive-bench harness (adapters for Boost message queue and Open MPI are small C++/C helper programs under third_party/).
claimed_speedup: Read from the chart labels in assets/bench-pingpong-throughput-1kb.png (1 KB, 1p1c, msgs/sec): Myelon-Raw mmap 4.9M and shm 4.4M vs Boost-MQ 164K (about 27x to 30x, derived from page data) and Open MPI 2.0M (about 2.2x to 2.5x, derived from page data); iceoryx2 1.4M, Aeron (rusteron) 2.6M, crossbeam 2.6M, shmipc 60K, ZeroMQ-IPC 25K, ZeroMQ-TCP 14K.
compiler_and_flags: Boost-MQ helper: g++ -O3 -std=c++17 -pthread -march=native -flto -DNDEBUG (third_party/boost_pingpong/Makefile). Open MPI helper: mpicc -O3 -std=c11 -march=native -flto. Rust side: cargo profile 'competitive' with opt-level 3, fat LTO, codegen-units 1, panic abort (Cargo.toml); no target-cpu setting or .cargo/config.toml was found, so only the C++ and C helpers use -march=native.
hardware: README headline tables: AMD Ryzen 7 5800X (8C/16T, 4.85 GHz boost), 64 GiB DDR4, Ubuntu 22.04, kernel 6.8, via crates/perf-bench; the chart's machine is not stated separately.
stars_or_usage: 20 stars; myelon crate about 358 crates.io downloads
tradeoffs: Linux and macOS only. Fixed-size frames chosen at compile time (FixedFrame<N>), consumers busy-spin and burn a core each, and the crate does non-trivial unsafe work internally behind a safe API. Rust only: the README roadmap leaves 'C / C++' unchecked, so a C++ project would need FFI or a separate process. Framing, codecs and typed zero-copy cost throughput: the README's framed 1 KB ping-pong table gives 2.45M ops/s against the chart's 4.4M to 4.9M for the raw ring.
caveats: The headline win is mostly a wait-strategy gap: the Boost helper uses blocking message_queue send and receive (a shared-memory queue guarded by an interprocess mutex and condition variable, per the Boost.Interprocess design), while Myelon busy-spins on atomics, so 27x to 30x measures spinning against blocking, not Rust against C++. Numbers exist only as chart labels (no results table in the repo text), read from the PNG; single run, no variance shown, and the chart's hardware is inferred from the README's headline-numbers paragraph. The harness is the project's own (first party). Open MPI is run through a 'vader self' adapter, a shared-memory path of an MPI library, not a purpose-built ring. This is an IPC transport rather than a general concurrency runtime, so the category fit is loose. Last commit is May 2026; the repo has 106 commits.
found_via: crates.io API harvest of concurrency keyword queries, then a grep of crate READMEs for C++ comparator names; the Myelon README listing 'Boost.MQ, OpenMPI' adapters surfaced it; opened README.md, the competitive-bench README, SETUP.md and Makefile, third_party/boost_pingpong/Makefile and main.cpp, third_party/ompi_pingpong/Makefile, Cargo.toml and the 1 KB ping-pong chart.
why_faster: README: LMAX Disruptor design extended to cross-process IPC with lock-free atomics, no syscalls in the hot path, cache-aligned cursors and busy-spin waiting; the Boost-MQ peer waits on a mutex and condition variable instead of spinning.

name: Kairos / rusty_rtos_kernel (FreeRTOS kernel remade in Rust)
baseline: FreeRTOS V11.3.1 kernel (C), unmodified, with its first-party GCC RISC-V port, built with clang -O2
workload: Retired instructions per call on RV32IMAC under QEMU virt with -icount shift=0, same operations in both kernels (tick, scheduler selection, whole task switch, list operation), plus RAM per task and flash size; both kernels are first proven trace-identical on 22 conformance scenarios.
claimed_speedup: rv32 retired instructions, Kairos vs FreeRTOS: tick 9 vs 15 (0.60x); cooperative switch (yield, block, take) 75 vs 110 (0.68x); list operation 18.47 vs 22.32 (0.83x); RAM per task 176 B vs 596 B (0.30x). Against Kairos in the same table: preemptive switch 119 vs 110 (1.08x), scheduler selection alone 45 vs 27 (1.67x), flash 19,484 B vs 13,924 B (1.40x). README says thirteen rows have a C arm: ten win or match, three are against Kairos.
compiler_and_flags: Both arms clang -target riscv32-unknown-elf -march=rv32imac -mabi=ilp32 -O2, no LTO on either side (bench/tick-work/run.sh and README); Rust arm built with cargo run --release in firmware/riscv32-qemu-tick-work.
hardware: QEMU virt emulating rv32imac with -icount shift=0 (deterministic retired-instruction counter); host CPU not stated; ESP32-S3 silicon cycle figures exist for Kairos only, with no C arm.
stars_or_usage: 0 stars (kernel repo), 1 star (kairos umbrella repo); rusty_rtos_kernel crate about 424 crates.io downloads
tradeoffs: Flash is 1.40x larger (handle validation, stackless resume machinery, u16 list ids); queue items are at most 8 bytes; SMP only on two cores with no affinity; no MPU, no static allocation and no co-routines; no privilege separation between tasks; a C ABI crate (rusty_rtos-capi) lets unmodified FreeRTOS C demos link against it.
caveats: Metric is retired instructions under an emulator, not wall-clock time or cycles, and no host CPU model is given; the C baseline is built -O2 (not -O3). The project's own text warns the cooperative-switch win is about where a yield is taken (FreeRTOS's RISC-V portYIELD() is an ecall trap) and not cheaper register moves; on Cortex-M3 the PendSV handler is 19 vs 19 instructions (parity). Mixed result: preemptive switch, scheduler selection and flash are worse than the C. The umbrella repo's bench/tick-work/README.md header block still shows older numbers (tick 56 vs 15, 3.73x worse; whole cooperative switch 109 vs 110) that contradict the current README table (tick 9 vs 15), so the numbers were moved after the bench README was last regenerated. The project's ledger records an earlier silicon harness defect that was corrected. First-party only, no independent measurement, near-zero adoption. An RTOS scheduler is a loose fit for the concurrency-runtimes category.
found_via: crates.io API harvest ('rtos', 'scheduler kernel' and concurrency queries), then a README grep for 'vs C' comparison tables; opened the kairos umbrella README, bench/tick-work/run.sh and README, docs/LEDGER.md, rusty_rtos_kernel README and rusty_rtos_core README, and the GitHub repo and commits pages.
why_faster: README: FreeRTOS pays 110 instructions for every RISC-V switch because its portYIELD() is a trap that saves everything an interrupt could clobber, while Kairos yields cooperatively for 75; the stackless task design removes the per-task stack (RAM); the project itself says the cooperative gain is about where the yield is taken, not about moving registers more cheaply.
